items.source_title: DeepSWE: The Coding Agent Benchmark That Fixes SWE-bench's Blind Spots
items.short_factual_summary: Tokoscope describes DeepSWE as a coding-agent benchmark built from original long-horizon tasks across active open-source repositories, using behavior-focused prompts and program-based verifiers rather than issue-derived tasks or LLM-as-judge scoring.
items.why_it_matters_for_ai_assisted_developme: The local practice signal is that software-engineering evals should resist contamination and over-specified prompts, require repository exploration, and attach cost-per-task evidence to pass rates.
items.local_practice_implication: Candidate evidence for trajectory-level evaluation, benchmark realism, contamination controls, and cost-aware agent eval reporting.
follow_up_notes: During ingest, route model leaderboard details upstream and keep the local synthesis to benchmark design practice.

items.source_title: How to Pick an Open-Source AI Coding Agent: 9 Tools, Four Different Jobs
items.short_factual_summary: The guide compares open-source coding agents by workflow surface, license, privacy, setup, costs, permission policy, and failure mode, and frames selection around IDE supervision, terminal loops, Git-controlled edits, and autonomous queues.
items.why_it_matters_for_ai_assisted_developme: This is a practice-level selection frame: choose the agent surface by supervision model, repository-context exposure, queue ownership, approval behavior, and Git evidence rather than by product popularity alone.
items.local_practice_implication: Candidate source for operating-model guidance on tool selection by supervision surface, permissions, network exposure, and source-control evidence.
follow_up_notes: Avoid creating local product comparison leaves; extract the reusable selection criteria.

items.source_title: The Multi-Agent Auditability Gap: Why Codex CLI's Encrypted Sub-Agent Delegation Is a Compliance Liability
items.date_basis: Article page shows July 25, 2026 and Updated July 25, 2026.
items.short_factual_summary: The article argues that encrypted sub-agent delegation payloads leave local logs with evidence that a delegation occurred but not the delegated instruction text, reducing inspectability for debugging, compliance, and audit trails.
items.why_it_matters_for_ai_assisted_developme: Multi-agent workflow records need enough task-decomposition evidence to reconstruct who delegated what, to whom, under which authority, and with which review outcome.
items.local_practice_implication: Candidate evidence for subagent audit logs, delegation-chain records, and approval evidence requirements.
follow_up_notes: Treat the article as a downstream governance lens; verify primary product and legal details before durable claims.

items.date_basis: Stats page shows Last updated: July 26, 2026 at 10:58 PM UTC and says data refreshes hourly.
items.short_factual_summary: The stats page reports opt-in developer usage logs across eight AI coding tools, including estimated aggregate spend, token volume, per-tool cost share, developer counts, and active days.
items.why_it_matters_for_ai_assisted_developme: Agent adoption needs cost and token telemetry at the tool and workflow level so teams can detect outlier spend, compare task surfaces, and budget agent use by outcome rather than license count.
items.local_practice_implication: Candidate source for agent cost telemetry, usage ledgers, and per-tool operating model dashboards.
follow_up_notes: Opt-in community telemetry may be skewed; use it as a practice signal, not a representative market metric.

items.source_title: AI Moved into the Dev Workflow. Security Didn't.
items.short_factual_summary: The article frames AI coding systems as increasingly autonomous development agents that can make architecture decisions, generate tests, and ship changes, creating visibility gaps for security teams when work happens outside centralized review processes.
items.why_it_matters_for_ai_assisted_developme: Security governance should follow the agent workflow itself: generation, testing, review, merge, and deployment records need policy checks and visibility before AI-authored volume scales.
items.local_practice_implication: Candidate support for AI-assisted security review gates, traceability, and centralized review visibility.
follow_up_notes: During ingest, separate general security-market framing from concrete local workflow controls.

items.source_title: AI Product Updates, July 26: Athena, Voice-Controlled Coding Agents, and More
items.short_factual_summary: The roundup notes Openbase voice dispatch, steering, and approval for asynchronous coding agents, CodexBar Lite as a macOS monitor for Codex CLI usage, and a hackathon pattern that makes disagreement and refusal part of an agent architecture.
items.why_it_matters_for_ai_assisted_developme: Asynchronous coding-agent supervision is moving beyond chat prompts into voice steering, usage monitors, explicit refusal paths, and multi-agent council patterns that need auditable decision records.
items.local_practice_implication: Candidate evidence for streaming progress, supervision channels, refusal-as-signal, and lightweight usage monitors.
follow_up_notes: Treat product launches as upstream-owned; local durable content should focus on supervision and refusal workflow patterns.

items.date_basis: Page header shows July 26, 2026 Research Brief.
items.short_factual_summary: The research brief identifies a shift from model-only evaluation toward system-level deployment-aware testing across runtimes, retrieval, memory, tool workflows, human review, runtime constraints, cost, latency, abstention, and calibration.
items.why_it_matters_for_ai_assisted_developme: Local verification should evaluate the full coding-agent system: retrieval routing, memory behavior, tool authorization, runtime containment, human escalation, and recoverability, not only final answer correctness.
items.local_practice_implication: Candidate support for deployment-aware evals, gated autonomy, retrieval-risk reviews, and runtime/tool orchestration tests.
follow_up_notes: Route broad paper coverage upstream; extract local practice guidance on harness design and retrieval/tool failure modes.

items.source_title: Claude Code Memory, Explained: CLAUDE.md, Auto Memory, and What They Miss
items.short_factual_summary: The article distinguishes repository instruction files from auto memory, describes local and project-scoped memory boundaries, and notes that memories and transcripts can become isolated by tool, machine, and repository.
items.why_it_matters_for_ai_assisted_developme: Durable agent instructions and memory need explicit scope boundaries: team-shared repo conventions, private local preferences, cross-tool continuity, and searchable decision history should not be conflated.
items.local_practice_implication: Candidate evidence for context-memory lifecycle, durable instruction scope, and private-vs-shared memory governance.
follow_up_notes: Avoid product-specific memory claims unless primary docs confirm them; local synthesis should cover scope separation and governance.

items.source_title: How to Use OpenCode CLI with OpenRouter
items.short_factual_summary: The tutorial describes initializing a terminal coding agent so it creates an AGENTS.md or OpenCode.md context file, attaching files into prompts, granting bash/file permissions, and using a model-router service for provider failover.
items.why_it_matters_for_ai_assisted_developme: The practice signal is that provider failover and model routing should be governed like part of the agent runtime, with permission prompts, generated instruction files, and context attachment treated as auditable setup actions.
items.local_practice_implication: Candidate source for setup-prompt governance, generated instruction review, model-router failover controls, and terminal-agent permission prompts.
follow_up_notes: Use cautiously as a tutorial source; verify tool specifics against primary docs before durable product claims.
